videos.title: Grip that does not fight the racket
videos.description: Neutral grip and quick shifts for clears vs net — without death-gripping the handle.

notes.abstract: A relaxed neutral grip lets you change faces fast; a tight fist slows every transition.
points: Hold the racket as if shaking hands, not squeezing a hammer.
Practice silent grip changes before the shuttle arrives.
Keep the ready position with the racket head up.
notes.conclusion: If net shots feel clumsy, check grip tension before footwork.

videos.title: Serve that starts the rally on purpose
videos.description: High serve vs low serve: when to push deep and when to keep it tight.

notes.abstract: Serves set the geometry of the next two shots — choose height and depth with intent.
points: Low serve: skim the tape and land early in the service box.
High serve: push deep to buy recovery time.
Watch the receiver’s base before you choose.
notes.conclusion: A random serve is free points for your opponent — pick a plan each time.

videos.title: Footwork to the four corners
videos.description: Split step, push, and recover to center without extra steps.

notes.abstract: Good footwork is a split-step plus a committed push, then a recovery path home.
points: Time the split step with the opponent’s contact.
Push with the outside leg toward the shuttle.
Recover toward center, not toward the sideline you just left.
notes.conclusion: Late feet make even good strokes look weak — move first, swing second.

videos.title: Clear, drop, and the mid-court lie
videos.description: Building an intermediate rally vocabulary so you are not stuck only clearing.

notes.abstract: Clears buy time; drops punish a deep base — alternate so your opponent cannot camp.
points: Use clears when you need recovery.
Drop when they sit deep after a high shot.
Disguise the preparation so both options look similar early.
notes.conclusion: One-paced clears are readable — change height and timing.

videos.title: Smash with a landing plan
videos.description: Jump smash mechanics and why recovery matters more than peak speed.

notes.abstract: A smash only scores if you can stand the reply — contact quality plus landing balance.
points: Reach high and hit down the line or into space.
Land ready to defend the block.
Do not smash every mid-court gift if you are off-balance.
notes.conclusion: Uncontrolled smashes gift the next shuttle — attack with an exit.

videos.title: Low center of gravity, then rise to hit
videos.description: Coach Liu on center-of-gravity control for full-court movement — stay low while moving, rise into the hit, then drop low again. Original: 重心上下前后不会转换？教练：一节课讲透重心控制，全场跑位不再东倒西歪！

notes.abstract: Beginner footwork height control: low center of gravity while moving, stand up into the hit, then drop low again and recover with circle movement.
points: When you are moving, keep a low center of gravity.
When you hit, get up into the shot.
After hitting, drop low again and recover with circle movement.
Stay balanced front-to-back so you are not tumbling through court transitions.
notes.conclusion: If you stay high while running or stay low through contact, timing and recovery both suffer — change height with the phase.

videos.title: Net touch: frame set, hand at tape height
videos.description: Coach Liu on net technique — frame set, hand level with the tape, stable soft net shots and receives. Original: 网前总被推个跟头？教练：框架摆好、手与网袋平齐，搓球接球全都稳！

notes.abstract: Beginner net play: set a stable racket frame, keep the hand near net-tape height, and use soft touch so you are not shoved off balance at the net.
points: Set a stable racket frame before contact — don’t poke with a floppy wrist.
Keep the hitting hand near net-tape height so soft net shots stay controlled.
Use a soft rubbing / touch action at the net instead of a hard swing.
Prepare early for the next contact — recovery starts as you finish the net shot.
notes.conclusion: Watch once for the shape, then drill the same contact with fewer shuttles and cleaner balance.

resorts.name: Community indoor hall
resorts.summary: Beginner-friendly booking, multiple courts, evening peaking times.
resorts.intro:
Look for halls with clear court lines, decent lighting, and a way to book a court rather than only drop-in chaos.

Evenings fill fast — early slots are better for drills.

Bring non-marking shoes; many halls are strict.

resorts.name: Competition training center
resorts.summary: Faster play, coaching lanes, and higher court fees.
resorts.intro:
Competition centers suit intermediate players who want pace and structured drills.

Expect stricter etiquette and less casual multi-shuttle chaos.

Good for match practice once basics are stable.
